subject: Cognitive Science
title: Premortem Analysis
description: A micro-lesson that makes Premortem Analysis usable.

hook.text: Before starting a project, imagine it has failed spectacularly. Now explain why. This is a premortem.

buildup.text: Gary Klein invented the technique: projecting failure makes hidden risks visible before they strike.

discovery.text: It works because it gives people permission to voice doubts. In a regular meeting, dissent feels risky.

twist.text: Groups running premortems identify 30% more risks than groups using standard planning methods.

climax.text: The premortem flips optimism bias on its head. Instead of asking 'how will we succeed,' you ask 'how did we fail.'

punchline.text: Imagining failure is the best way to prevent it.

quiz.question: What is a premortem?
options: Imagining a project has failed and analyzing why
An autopsy of a past failure

details.summary: Gary Klein's premortem technique asks teams to imagine a project has failed and then explain why. Unlike postmortems, premortems leverage prospective hindsight to surface risks before they materialize. This overcomes groupthink and overconfidence by making failure concrete and discussable.
details.whyItMatters: Premortems turn wishful thinking into risk management. By legitimizing pessimism before a decision is finalized, they improve planning and prevent avoidable failures.
takeaways: Teams imagine the project has failed and explain why
Prospective hindsight makes risks easier to identify

faq.question: How does a premortem differ from a postmortem?
faq.answer: A postmortem investigates what went wrong after failure. A premortem imagines failure before it happens. Because the failure is hypothetical, team members feel free to voice concerns without seeming disloyal or pessimistic. It shifts the social dynamic from consensus to constructive critique.

faq.question: How do you run a premortem effectively?
faq.answer: Have everyone independently write reasons the project failed, then share and discuss. This prevents anchoring on the leader's concerns. The key is making failure hypothetical but vivid, using phrases like imagine it is six months from now and we failed. Anonymity helps surface uncomfortable truths.
